decisions.choice: love: the two verbs for love in 21:15-17 (ἀγαπάω, used by Jesus in his first two questions, and φιλέω, used by Peter in all three answers and by Jesus in the third question) are taken as having the same meaning here
alternatives: a distinction is meant: Jesus first asks for the fullest, self-giving love (ἀγαπάω), Peter can only answer with the love of a friend (φιλέω), and the third time Jesus comes down to Peter's own word
decisions.reason: John uses both verbs for the same love again and again: for the Father's love for the Son (3:35 ἀγαπᾷ; 5:20 φιλεῖ), for Jesus's love for Lazarus (11:5 ἠγάπα; 11:3 and 11:36 ἐφίλει), and for the disciple whom Jesus loved (13:23 ἠγάπα; 20:2 ἐφίλει). In this same passage he also varies the words for feeding and shepherding, for lambs and sheep, and for knowing (verses 15-17), with no change of sense. And verse 17 says Peter was grieved because Jesus asked a third time, not because he changed the verb. Still, the change of verb in the third question can be read as deliberate, and a footnote gives that view.

decisions.choice: more than these others love me
alternatives: more than you love these others
more than these things: the boat, the nets and the fishing (21:3)
decisions.reason: "These" can be masculine or neuter, and the comparison can be with what they do or with what Peter loves. Six other disciples are there (21:2), and Peter had once claimed a loyalty greater than theirs: he would lay down his life for Jesus (13:37; compare Mark 14:29, where he says he will stand firm even if all the others fall away). The question would then ask whether that claim still stands after his denials. But the words can also ask whether Peter loves Jesus more than he loves his friends, or more than the fishing he has just gone back to (21:3). In his reply Peter does not compare himself with anyone.

decisions.choice: son of John (SBLGNT), as in 1:42 and in verses 16 and 17
alternatives: son of Jonah, or Jonas (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts read John here, as at 1:42; many later ones read Jonah, as in Matthew 16:17 ("Bar-Jonah"). This John is Peter's father, not John the Baptist. Jesus uses Peter's full name, the name he had when Jesus first met him (1:42), not the name Peter that Jesus gave him. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the meal by the charcoal fire recalls the night of Peter's denials
decisions.reason: Jesus has just given the disciples breakfast of bread and fish by a charcoal fire (21:9-13). The word for a charcoal fire (ἀνθρακιά) is used in the New Testament only here (21:9) and at 18:18, where Peter stood warming himself and denied Jesus. Jesus now asks him three times about his love, as Peter had three times said he was not a disciple (18:17, 25-27).

decisions.choice: says (L); said (B, R); also in verses 15, 16, 17 and 19
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("he says") to make a scene vivid. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in English. This applies to every "says" in the passage (verses 15, 16, 17 and 19). "Said" in verse 17 is already a past tense in Greek.

decisions.choice: love, for both verbs, at every level
alternatives: love (for the first verb) and be fond of, or love as a friend (for the second)
decisions.reason: Both verbs are "love" throughout John (meaning decision m1), so they are "love" here too, at Literal as well. To give them different English words would decide the question the footnote leaves open, and would make Peter's answer sound weaker than it need be.

decisions.choice: more than these others do (R); Jesus spoke to Simon Peter ... he said
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "more than these", which leaves the comparison open. Readable says what meaning decision m2 finds most likely, so it is marked uncertain.

decisions.choice: historic present at Literal ("dice"); pretérito at Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in John: Literal keeps the present tense in which John tells these past events; Balanced and Readable use the pretérito, as Spanish tells a story. This applies to every "dice" in the passage (verses 15, 16, 17 and 19).

decisions.choice: amar, for both Greek verbs for love, at every level (verses 15-17)
decisions.reason: Both verbs are "love" throughout John (meaning decision m1), so Spanish says "amar" for both, at Literal as well, and the alternation is not shown in the text. To give the second verb a different word ("querer", "tener cariño") would decide the question that the footnote on m1 leaves open, and would make Peter's answer sound weaker than it need be.

decisions.choice: Simón, [hijo] de Juan (L); Simón, hijo de Juan (B, R)
decisions.reason: The same name as at 1:42 (meaning decision m3); Literal brackets "hijo", which the Greek leaves understood. "Me" is a clitic and takes no setting.

decisions.choice: más de lo que me aman estos otros (R); Le preguntó (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "más que estos", which leaves the comparison open. Readable says what meaning decision m2 finds most likely, so it is marked uncertain.

decisions.choice: narration in the passé simple (L, B), with Literal keeping John's present tense ("Jésus dit", "il lui dit"); passé composé (R); speech in the present and passé composé at every level
alternatives: passé composé for narration at every level
the present tense throughout at Literal
decisions.reason: The French brief for the whole passage (21:15-19). The passé simple ("Pierre fut attristé") is the normal tense of written narrative and suits a public reading; Literal uses it for the Greek past tenses and keeps the present where John tells a past event in the present (every "il lui dit" in verses 15-17 and 19), as the English Literal does; with "dire" the present and the passé simple look the same. Balanced turns the questions into "il lui demanda" and Readable uses the passé composé ("Jésus a demandé") throughout.

decisions.choice: "aimer" for both Greek verbs, at every level, in verses 15-17; French does not show the alternation in the text
alternatives: "aimer" for the first verb and "avoir de l'affection pour" or "aimer d'amitié" for the second
decisions.reason: Meaning decision m1 takes the two verbs as meaning the same here, so French uses its one ordinary verb for love for both, as the English uses "love". A second French verb would decide the question that the footnote on m1 leaves open, and every candidate would make Peter's answer sound weaker or more sentimental: "avoir de l'affection" is less than love, "aimer d'amitié" is heavy, and "chérir" is literary. The reader who wants to know which Greek verb stands where finds it in the footnote and in the meaning decisions on verses 15, 16 and 17.

decisions.choice: plus que ceux-ci (L, B); plus que les autres ne m'aiment (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek "these" can be masculine or neuter (meaning decision m2). French must choose a gender: "ceux-ci" points to the other disciples, the reading m2 prefers, and still leaves open whether they are the ones who love or the ones loved; "cela" would point to the boat and the nets. Readable says the most likely sense outright, as the English Readable does.

decisions.choice: historic present kept at Literal ("anamwambia"); -li- then -ka- at Balanced; plain past at Readable
decisions.reason: John tells this conversation in the present tense ("he says", verses 15, 16, 17 and 19). Literal keeps it, as the English Literal does; Balanced uses -li- for the first verb of a sequence and -ka- for those that follow, as written Swahili narrative does, and Readable tells it in the plain past. This holds for the whole passage.

decisions.choice: "kupenda" for both verbs for love in verses 15-17, at every level
alternatives: "kupenda" for one verb and "kuwa na upendo wa kirafiki" or "kuthamini" for the other
decisions.reason: Both Greek verbs are "love" throughout John and are taken to mean the same here (meaning decision m1). Swahili has one plain verb for love, "kupenda", so the alternation between the two Greek verbs is not shown in the text; the footnote on meaning decision m1 gives it, and the view that a distinction is meant. A second Swahili word would decide that question and make Peter's answer sound weaker than it need be. "Unanipenda" and "nakupenda" stay the same in all three questions and answers.

decisions.choice: "yêu" for both agapan and philein in 21:15-17
alternatives: "yêu thương" for agapan and "thương mến" for philein
decisions.reason: Follows the meaning decision that the two verbs mean the same here; using one Vietnamese verb keeps that reading. A reviewer may prefer to mark the change of verb.

decisions.choice: Jesus says "Ta" and calls Peter "con"; "con trai Giăng" for "of John"
decisions.reason: "con trai" keeps "son of John" apart from "con", the word Jesus uses for "you" to a disciple (style guide section 6).

decisions.choice: "사랑하다" for both Greek verbs (agapaō and phileō) throughout 21:15-17, at every level
alternatives: "사랑하다" for agapaō and "좋아하다" or "아끼다" for phileō
decisions.reason: As docs/john-terms.md and the meaning decision: John uses both verbs of the Father's love for the Son, so the change is most likely style. Any second Korean verb would be weaker than "사랑하다" and would make Peter's answers sound like a step down, which the text need not mean. Some readers hold that a distinction is meant; the footnote gives that view.

decisions.choice: historic present "말씀하신다", "말씀드린다" (L); past tense (B, R), through 21:15-19
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek present in narrative; Balanced and Readable use the past. One decision for the passage.

vi.B: Phi-e-rơ thưa với {{deity_pronoun:ngài|Ngài}}: "Vâng, lạy Chúa, Chúa biết con yêu Chúa."

ko.L: 그가 그분께 말씀드린다. "예, 주님, 제가 주님을 사랑하는 줄 주님께서 아십니다."
ko.B: 베드로가 대답했다. "예, 주님. 제가 주님을 사랑하는 것을 주님께서 아십니다."
ko.R: "예, 주님. 제가 주님을 사랑한다는 것을 주님께서 아십니다." 하고 베드로가 대답했다.

decisions.choice: you know: Peter appeals to what Jesus himself knows
decisions.reason: "You" is stressed in Greek. After his denials Peter does not offer his own word as proof; he rests on Jesus's knowledge of him, which John has shown before (1:47-48; 2:24-25).

decisions.choice: Yes, I love you: Peter answers about his love but not about "more than these"
decisions.reason: Peter says yes to loving Jesus but makes no claim to love him more than the others. The man who once promised to lay down his life (13:37) now claims less. The verb he uses is the other verb for love (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: Lord: Peter's address to his risen master
decisions.reason: The disciples call Jesus "Lord" throughout John (6:68; 13:36-37), and in this chapter the disciple whom Jesus loved has just recognized him: "It is the Lord" (21:7).

decisions.choice: Peter said (B); Peter answered (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker so that the reader can follow who is speaking. Readable starts a new sentence at "You know", so that "You" takes a capital in any case.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:tú|Tú}} sabes; Pedro (B, R)
decisions.reason: Spanish can leave the subject in the verb, so writing "tú" keeps the stress of the Greek pronoun (meaning decision m1); as a pronoun for Christ it takes the reader setting, except where Readable starts a new sentence with it. "Te" is a clitic and takes no setting. Balanced and Readable name Peter as the speaker.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:toi|Toi}}, {{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} sais (L)
decisions.reason: The Greek "you" is stressed (meaning decision m1). French shows the stress by doubling the pronoun with "toi", which Literal does here and in verse 17; Balanced and Readable keep the plain "tu sais". Readable starts a new sentence at "Tu sais", so the pronoun there is written plainly with its capital.

decisions.choice: Bwana; {{deity_pronoun:wewe|Wewe}} unajua (L, B); Unajua (R)
alternatives: unajua, without the pronoun, at every level
decisions.reason: Peter stresses "you" (meaning decision m1), so Literal and Balanced keep the free pronoun "wewe", which carries the reader setting for pronouns for Christ; "-ku-" in "nakupenda" is inside the verb and has none. Readable leaves the stress to the verb. "Bwana" is capitalised, as the address of a disciple to the risen Jesus.

decisions.choice: Peter addresses Jesus as "Chúa" for "you" and calls himself "con"; "lạy Chúa" (L, B), "thưa Chúa" (R)
decisions.reason: A disciple who calls Jesus "Lord" (kyrie) uses "Chúa" as the noun of address, as docs/john-terms.md sets; it takes no setting span.

decisions.choice: Peter speaks in 합쇼체 and says "주님" for "you"; Jesus answers in 해라체
decisions.reason: Disciples speak to Jesus formally and call him "주님" (style guide, section 4); Korean does not use "당신" to a revered person, so the stressed "you know" becomes "주님께서 아십니다". This holds for all three answers.

fr.R: Jésus lui a dit : « Nourris {{deity_pronoun:mes|Mes}} agneaux. »

vi.B: Đức Giê-xu bảo ông: "Hãy nuôi các chiên con của {{deity_pronoun:ta|Ta}}."
vi.R: Đức Giê-xu bảo ông: "Hãy nuôi những chiên con của {{deity_pronoun:ta|Ta}}."

ko.L: 그분이 그에게 말씀하신다. "내 어린 양들을 먹여라."
ko.B: 예수께서 그에게 말씀하셨다. "내 어린 양들을 먹여라."
ko.R: 예수께서 그에게 말씀하셨다. "내 어린 양들을 먹여라."

decisions.choice: the lambs are the people who belong to Jesus; Peter is given a shepherd's work
decisions.reason: Jesus has called himself the good shepherd and his followers his sheep (10:11-16). He calls them "my" lambs: they remain his, and Peter is to care for them on his behalf. In the Scriptures God holds the shepherds of his people to account for feeding the flock (Ezekiel 34:2-16; Jeremiah 23:1-4), and Peter later gives the same charge to the elders of the churches (1 Peter 5:2).

decisions.choice: lambs: young sheep, standing here for the flock as a whole
alternatives: only the young or weak believers, as distinct from the sheep of verses 16-17
decisions.reason: The word (ἀρνίον) is used only here in John's Gospel. It is a different word from "the Lamb of God" in 1:29. Jesus goes on to say "sheep" in verses 16 and 17 with no sign of a change of flock; the variation is most likely one of style (see the decision on verse 17).

decisions.choice: Jesus said
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus as the speaker, since the last speaker was Peter.

decisions.choice: Apacienta (L, B) / Alimenta (R) for the verb of verses 15 and 17; Pastorea (L, B) / Cuida ... como un pastor (R) for the verb of verse 16
decisions.reason: Spanish has a verb for each Greek verb: "apacentar" is to lead a flock to pasture and feed it, and "pastorear" is to do a shepherd's whole work, which keeps the link with the good shepherd of 10:11-16 (meaning decision m1 at verse 16). One Spanish verb for both would hide the variation that verse 17 discusses. "Apacentar" is a little formal, so Readable says "alimentar". "Mis" is a possessive and takes no setting.

decisions.choice: Jesús le dijo
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus as the speaker, since the last speaker was Peter.

decisions.choice: Fais paître (L, B); Nourris (R)
decisions.reason: The verb is the one for feeding a flock at pasture (meaning decision m1). "Faire paître" says that plainly; the old imperative "Pais" is now rare and sounds archaic. Readable says "Nourris". The verb stays distinct from "Sois le berger de" in verse 16, as the two Greek verbs are, and returns in verse 17.

decisions.choice: wanakondoo (lambs), at every level
decisions.reason: "Wanakondoo" is the ordinary Swahili for lambs. It is the same word as in "Mwanakondoo wa Mungu" (1:29), though the Greek words differ (meaning decision m2); a reader may hear a link that the Greek does not make. "Kondoo wachanga" (young sheep) would avoid it but is less natural. A reviewer may prefer it.

decisions.choice: "nuôi" for boskein (verses 15, 17); "chăn" for poimainein (verse 16)
decisions.reason: Keeps the variation of the Greek, which the meaning decision reads as one charge in varied words.

decisions.choice: "어린 양들" (two words) for lambs
decisions.reason: "어린양" written as one word is the title "Lamb of God" (1:29); here the word is the ordinary young sheep standing for Jesus's flock, written as two words.

decisions.choice: A second time he asked him (B); For the second time Jesus asked him (R)

decisions.choice: shepherd: do all of a shepherd's work, leading, guarding and providing for the flock
decisions.reason: The verb (ποιμαίνω) is wider than "feed" (βόσκω, verses 15 and 17): it covers the whole care of a shepherd for the flock. It shares a root with "shepherd" in 10:11-16, so Jesus gives Peter a share in his own work as the good shepherd. Peter uses the same verb when he charges the elders to shepherd God's flock (1 Peter 5:2).

decisions.choice: sheep (SBLGNT)
alternatives: little sheep: a diminutive form of the word (some early manuscripts, among them Codex Vaticanus)
decisions.reason: Some important early manuscripts read a diminutive form, "little sheep", here and in verse 17; others read the ordinary word for sheep, as the SBLGNT does. A diminutive like this was often used with no difference in meaning, so the sense is the same either way: the people who belong to Jesus (10:3-4, 14-16). A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Shepherd (L, B); Take care of ... as a shepherd does (R)
decisions.reason: "Shepherd" as a verb keeps the link with the good shepherd of 10:11-16 and keeps the two verbs of verses 15-17 apart (meaning decision m1). "Tend" is less common in everyday English. Readable spells out the picture in plain words.

decisions.choice: Pastorea (L, B); Cuida de ... como un pastor (R); ovejas
decisions.reason: The wider shepherd's verb (meaning decision m1), kept apart from "apacentar" in verses 15 and 17 (see the decision at verse 15). Readable spells out the picture in plain words. "Ovejas" is the word of 10:1-16.

decisions.choice: Sois le berger de (L, B); Prends soin de ... comme un berger (R); brebis
decisions.reason: French has no everyday verb for the whole of a shepherd's work (meaning decision m1): "paître" is feeding, and "garder" or "conduire" each give only one part. "Sois le berger de" uses the noun of "le bon berger" (10:11-16), which keeps the link the verb makes. "Brebis" is the word for the flock in chapter 10.

decisions.choice: "Lisha" (verses 15 and 17) and "Chunga" (verse 16), at every level
alternatives: Watunze kondoo wangu kama mchungaji afanyavyo (R)
decisions.reason: The two Greek verbs are kept apart, as in the English, so that "Lisha" in verses 15 and 17 frames "Chunga" here. "Kuchunga" is the whole work of a shepherd (meaning decision m1) and shares its root with "mchungaji" (shepherd), the word of 10:11-16 in this translation, so the link with the good shepherd is plain. Because "kuchunga" is an everyday verb, Readable keeps it and does not need the explanation the English Readable adds.

decisions.choice: "양들을 치다" (L, B); "목자처럼 돌보다" (R)
decisions.reason: "양을 치다" is the standard Korean for a shepherd's whole work and keeps the change from "feed" in verses 15 and 17; Readable spells it out, since young readers may take "치다" as "hit".

decisions.choice: love: Jesus now uses the verb Peter has been using, with the same meaning as before

decisions.choice: the third time: the last of three questions

decisions.choice: A third time he asked him (B); For the third time Jesus asked him (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 16: the present "says" becomes "asked" at Balanced and Readable because it introduces a question (rendering decision r-en-1 at 21:15). "Love" stays the same word as in verses 15 and 16 (rendering decision r-en-2 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: preguntó (B, R); ¿me amas?, as in verses 15 and 16

decisions.choice: aimer, as in verses 15 and 16

decisions.reason: Here Jesus takes up the verb Peter has used (meaning decision m1). French keeps "aimer", so the question reads exactly as before (see the French decision on verse 15); the change of the Greek verb is given in the meaning decisions and the footnote on verse 15.

decisions.choice: "yêu" again, though Jesus now uses philein

decisions.choice: Peter was grieved because he was asked a third time
decisions.reason: John gives the reason plainly: it was the third asking that hurt Peter. The verb (λυπέω) means to feel pain or sorrow, not to be offended.

decisions.choice: three questions recall Peter's three denials
decisions.reason: Peter had denied Jesus three times by a charcoal fire, as Jesus had foretold (13:38; 18:17, 25-27). Now, by another charcoal fire (21:9), Jesus asks him three times whether he loves him, and three times gives him the care of his flock. The third question would remind Peter of his third denial; it also lets him say three times what he had three times denied.

decisions.choice: the grief is at the third asking; whether the change of verb added to it is uncertain
alternatives: Peter was grieved because Jesus now used the other verb for love, as if doubting even the love Peter had claimed
decisions.reason: John repeats the question exactly as Jesus asked it the third time, with Peter's own verb. Those who see a distinction between the verbs take this as part of the hurt. But the sentence names "the third time" as the cause, not the choice of word (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: was hurt (B); felt very sad (R); Jesus asked (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Grieved" is formal in modern English. "Hurt" carries the pain of the Greek word without suggesting that Peter was offended; Readable uses the plainest words. Balanced and Readable name Jesus and say "asked", since "said" here introduces a question.

decisions.choice: Se entristeció (L); se sintió dolido (B); se puso muy triste (R); Jesús le preguntó (B, R)
decisions.reason: Each verb carries pain or sorrow without suggesting that Peter took offence (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable name Jesus and say "preguntó", since the verb introduces a question; at Literal the subject is in the verb, so there is no pronoun to mark.

decisions.choice: attristé (L); peiné (B); très triste (R)
decisions.reason: The verb is to feel pain or sorrow, not offence (meaning decision m1). "Vexé" would say that Peter was offended, and "blessé" can suggest wounded pride; "peiné" and "attristé" say sorrow. At Literal and Balanced the quoted question opens the sentence, so its pronoun is written plainly with its capital.

decisions.choice: the reason clause before "베드로는 근심하였다"
decisions.reason: Korean puts a reason before the main verb; the order changes within the verse and the meaning does not.

decisions.choice: you know all things: Peter confesses what the disciples had said in 16:30
decisions.reason: On the night before the cross the disciples said, "Now we know that you know all things" (16:30). John has shown again and again that Jesus knows what is in people (1:47-48; 2:24-25; 6:64; 13:11). Peter now stakes everything on that knowledge, not on his own record.

decisions.choice: the two verbs for "know" (οἶδας and γινώσκεις) mean the same here
alternatives: you know all things in general; you recognize, by experience, that I love you
decisions.reason: Peter uses two different verbs for "know" in one breath. John uses both of Jesus's knowledge (2:24-25; 13:3, 7), and this passage varies its words throughout (see the decision on verse 17, last sentence). The second verb can be taken as knowledge gained by seeing and experiencing, but nothing in the sentence requires it.

decisions.choice: I love you: Peter's answer is the same in substance as before
decisions.reason: Peter uses the same verb for love as in his first two answers (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: know ... know, at every level
decisions.reason: The same English verb for both, because they mean the same here (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable drop the opening "And" and use normal English order; they name Peter, Balanced with "replied" since he is answering; Readable starts a new sentence at the second "You know".

decisions.choice: sabes ... sabes, at every level
decisions.reason: The same Spanish verb for both Greek verbs, because they mean the same here (meaning decision m2). Literal keeps the Greek order "todas las cosas sabes tú". Each "tú" takes the reader setting except where Readable begins a sentence with it.

decisions.choice: feed / shepherd and lambs / sheep: one charge in varied words
alternatives: three distinct tasks or three different groups (young believers, mature believers, and so on)
decisions.reason: Across verses 15-17 John varies almost every word: two verbs for love (verse 15), two for "know" (verse 17), "feed" (βόσκω) and "shepherd" (ποιμαίνω), "lambs" (ἀρνίον) and "sheep" (πρόβατον). Each pair is close in meaning, and the passage gives no sign that the variations mark separate groups or tasks. Together they give one charge: care for those who belong to Jesus, as he cares for them (10:11-16).

decisions.choice: sheep (SBLGNT)
alternatives: little sheep: a diminutive form (some early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: As in verse 16 (meaning decision m2 there), some manuscripts read the diminutive "little sheep"; the sense is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Jesus's words run on into verse 18
decisions.reason: The charge to feed the sheep leads straight into Jesus's word about how Peter will end his life (verses 18-19); the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (10:11), and so will Peter.

decisions.choice: Feed, as in verse 15
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verse 15 gets the same English, so that "Feed" in verses 15 and 17 frames "Shepherd" in verse 16 as in the Greek. The quotation stays open because Jesus goes on speaking in verse 18.

decisions.choice: Apacienta (L, B); Alimenta (R), as in verse 15

decisions.choice: put on a belt: tie the long outer clothes up with a belt, ready to walk or work; done by another, it may also hint at being bound
alternatives: be tied up with ropes, as a prisoner
decisions.reason: People wore long, loose robes and fastened a belt round them before setting out or starting work (compare 13:4; Luke 12:35). A young man does this for himself and goes where he likes. When another does it for him, he is no longer free: the words fit a helpless old man being dressed, and they also fit a prisoner being bound and led away to die, which is how verse 19 explains them.

decisions.choice: stretch out your hands: most likely a veiled pointer to death by crucifixion
alternatives: the gesture of a helpless old man reaching out for someone to dress him and lead him
decisions.reason: Verse 19 says Jesus was showing by what kind of death Peter would glorify God, the phrase John used of Jesus's own crucifixion (12:33; 18:32). Greek and Roman writers sometimes spoke of the hands being stretched out of a person put on a cross, and Christian writers from about AD 200 onward say that Peter was crucified in Rome. Against this, the stretching out of the hands comes before the belt and the leading away, not after them. The words are a veiled saying, and the decision is marked uncertain.

decisions.choice: younger: when you were young, compared with now
decisions.reason: The word is the comparative of "young", contrasting Peter's earlier years with the old age to come (γηράσῃς, "you grow old"). It does not mean Peter is old now.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage.

decisions.choice: put a belt on / fasten a belt / tie a belt (for the verb of girding); carry (L), take (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Gird" is no longer everyday English. Saying "belt" keeps the picture of the Greek, which allows both dressing and binding (meaning decision m1), rather than choosing one. The verb for "carry" is also used of leading or bringing someone; Balanced and Readable say "take". Literal supplies "you" and "to go", which the Greek leaves understood.

decisions.choice: En verdad, en verdad te digo (L, B); Te digo la verdad (R)
alternatives: De cierto, de cierto te digo
decisions.reason: The book-wide Spanish rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; "te", since Jesus speaks to Peter alone.

decisions.choice: te ceñías / te ceñirá (L); te ajustabas el cinturón / te atará el cinturón (B); te ponías el cinturón / te atará el cinturón (R); llevará
decisions.reason: "Ceñir" is still understood in Spanish, as at 13:4, so Literal keeps it. Balanced and Readable name the belt, and "atar" for what another does keeps both pictures the Greek allows, dressing and binding (meaning decision m1), without choosing one. Literal brackets "te" and "ir", which the Greek leaves understood.

decisions.choice: En vérité, en vérité, je te le dis (L, B); Je te le dis, c'est la vérité (R)
alternatives: Amen, amen, je te le dis
Oui, vraiment, je te le dis
decisions.reason: The book-wide French rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage. Jesus speaks to Peter alone, so "je te le dis". Readable puts the pledge in plain words.

decisions.choice: te ceignais ... te ceindra (L); attachais ta ceinture ... attachera ta ceinture (B); mettais ta ceinture ... t'attachera une ceinture (R); te portera (L); te conduira, t'emmènera (B, R)
decisions.reason: Keeping the belt keeps the picture of the Greek, which fits both an old man being dressed and a prisoner being bound (meaning decision m1), where "habiller" or "lier" would choose one. Literal says "ceindre", the verb used for Peter in verse 7; Balanced and Readable say it with "ceinture". The verb for "carry" is also used of leading someone; Literal keeps "porter" and the other levels say "conduire" and "emmener".

decisions.choice: Kweli kweli nakuambia (L, B); Nakuambia ukweli (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage. "Nakuambia" (I tell you, one person) because the Greek "you" is singular: Jesus is speaking to Peter alone.

decisions.choice: kujifunga mshipi (put a belt on oneself); atakufunga mshipi (another will put a belt on you)
decisions.reason: As in the English, "belt" keeps the picture of the Greek rather than choosing between dressing and binding (meaning decision m1). In Swahili "atakufunga" also means "he will bind you", so the hint of a prisoner led away, which verse 19 explains, is heard as in the Greek. "Ulipotaka" for "you wanted", so that "kupenda" is kept for love in this passage.

decisions.choice: "Thật vậy, thật vậy, Ta nói với con" (L, B); "Ta nói thật với con" (R)
decisions.reason: The style guide's book-wide rendering of amen amen; "Ta" opens the Readable sentence and so is written plainly.

decisions.choice: "진실로 진실로 너에게 말한다" (L, B); "내가 분명히 말한다" (R), singular "너에게" to Peter
decisions.reason: The book-wide form (style guide, section 6), with the singular pronoun because Jesus speaks to Peter alone. One decision for this passage.

decisions.choice: "손을 뻗다" (stretch out the hands) at every level
decisions.reason: The meaning decision reads the words as a veiled pointer to crucifixion; "손을 뻗다" keeps the Greek picture without spelling it out, as the Greek does. "팔을 벌리다" would say too much, "손을 내밀다" suggests asking for help.

decisions.choice: the narrator explains Jesus's words, with the phrase used of Jesus's own death
decisions.reason: John steps out of the scene to tell the reader what Jesus meant, in nearly the same words he used of Jesus's death ("signifying by what kind of death he was about to die", 12:33; 18:32). Peter will die as his Lord died. "Signifying" means pointing to something by a hint rather than saying it outright.

decisions.choice: Peter's death will glorify God
decisions.reason: In John the cross is where the Son glorifies the Father (12:23-28; 13:31-32; 17:1, 4). Peter's death, faithful to the end, will also bring glory to God.

decisions.choice: Peter (B, R); Jesus said ... bring glory to God (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Peter, so that the second "he" is not taken as Jesus. Balanced keeps the wording of 12:33 ("He said this to show ..."). Readable names Jesus and says "bring glory to" for "glorify". It does not add "on a cross" as 12:33 does, because here the kind of death is less certain (meaning decision m2 at verse 18).

decisions.choice: Pedro (B, R); Jesús (R); glorificaría (L, B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Peter, so that the subject of "glorificaría" is not taken as Jesus. Balanced keeps the shape of its 12:33 ("Dijo esto para indicar qué clase de muerte"), the link of meaning decision m1. Every level keeps "glorificar", John's word. Readable does not add "en una cruz" as at 12:33, because here the kind of death is less certain (meaning decision m2 at verse 18).

decisions.choice: pour signifier (L); pour indiquer (B); pour montrer (R) par quelle mort ... glorifierait Dieu
decisions.reason: The wording follows the French of 12:33, where John uses the same phrase of Jesus's own death (meaning decision m1), so that each level lets the reader hear the echo. Readable keeps "glorifier", the book-wide word, where the English Readable says "bring glory to": in French the verb is plain enough. Balanced and Readable name Peter so that the second "il" is not taken as Jesus.

decisions.choice: akionyesha ni kwa kifo cha namna gani (L); kuonyesha ni kwa kifo cha namna gani (B, R)
decisions.reason: The narrator uses nearly the words of 12:33 and 18:32 about Jesus's own death (meaning decision m1), so the Swahili repeats the wording of 12:33, "akionyesha ni kifo cha namna gani". Balanced and Readable name Peter, as the English does; Readable says "kumletea Mungu utukufu" (bring glory to God) for "kutukuza".

decisions.choice: "Ngài" written plainly at the start of the sentence
decisions.reason: Where the pronoun opens a sentence its capital is required anyway, so the style guide writes it plainly; elsewhere Jesus is {{deity_pronoun:ngài|Ngài}} in the narrative and {{deity_pronoun:ta|Ta}} when he speaks.

decisions.choice: "하나님을 영광스럽게 하다" at every level, Readable included
alternatives: "하나님께 영광을 돌리다" (R), as the English Readable "bring glory to God"
decisions.reason: "영광스럽게 하다" is the key term for "glorify" (style guide, section 6) and is plain enough for Readable; keeping it ties Peter's death to Jesus's own glorification.

ko.B: 이 말씀을 하시고 나서 예수께서 그에게 말씀하셨다. "나를 따라라."

decisions.choice: Follow me: the call to discipleship, now including following Jesus in death
decisions.reason: Jesus called his first disciples with these words (1:43). On the last night he told Peter, "You cannot follow me now ... but later you will follow" (13:36), and he had said that whoever serves him must follow him, and where he is, his servant will be (12:24-26). Now, after foretelling Peter's death, Jesus renews the call: Peter will follow him in life and, in the end, in the way he dies.

decisions.choice: Follow: keep on following
decisions.reason: The command is in the present tense, which in Greek points to a continuing way of life, not a single step.

decisions.choice: told him (B); Then Jesus said to Peter (R)
decisions.reason: The present "says" becomes a past tense (rendering decision r-en-1 at 21:15). Readable names both persons and puts "After saying this" as "Then". Every level keeps the short "Follow me" of 1:43 and 13:36.

decisions.choice: Sígueme, at every level
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the short call of 1:43 and 13:36 (meaning decision m1). "Me" is a clitic and takes no setting. Readable names both persons.

decisions.choice: No deity_pronoun spans in Korean ("께서", the honorific -시-, "그분"), through 21:15-19
alternatives: deity_pronoun spans as in the English
decisions.reason: Korean has no capital letters, so the deity_pronoun setting has nothing to change (style guide, section 7); respect for Jesus is carried by "께서", the honorific -시- and "그분" at every level. Recorded once for this passage.
